Space Invaders

Tomohiro Nishikado’s arcade game for Taito made rows of two-frame bitmap aliens the first icons of video game pixel art.

Source
Wikipedia: Space Invaders
Creator
Tomohiro Nishikado for Taito; distributed outside Japan by Midway
Made

Style
Pixel Art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Game-like, nostalgic, crisp
Evidence
Based on the Wikipedia article and its cited sources. No image was inspected for this record: the game graphics are in copyright, and no open, verified image was found.
Reviewed
2 October 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Wikipedia calls Space Invaders a 1978 fixed shooter developed and published by Taito for arcades, released in Japan in July 1978 and abroad through Midway later that year. Wikipedia.

Nishikado created bitmap images of octopus-like aliens after The War of the Worlds, with other aliens after squids and crabs. After he drew the pixel art, he made a tool to animate two frames of movement for each character and adjusted the designs on screen with a light pen. Wikipedia.

The game runs on an Intel 8080 and draws raster graphics through a bitmapped framebuffer. The hardware could not show color, so the first releases have black-and-white graphics with strips of orange and green cellophane over parts of the screen. Wikipedia.

Wikipedia says the pixelated aliens “have become pop culture icons, sometimes representing video games as a whole”. Wikipedia.

Why it belongs

The two-frame aliens are the model for the style’s motion rule: animation steps between a few frames, with no easing.

The cellophane strips show that the first color in the style came from hardware limits, as bands of flat color, not shading.

Borrow

Animate small sprites with two frames that alternate in step with movement.

Color whole horizontal bands of a monochrome screen instead of shading single objects.
